eruptions.description: Catastrophic eruption. Destroyed the original island, killing ~36,000 people. The sound was heard 4,800 km away.
Emergence of Anak Krakatau ('Son of Krakatau') from the sea.
Flank collapse triggered a tsunami that killed 431 people in Java and Sumatra.
Explosive eruption with a 15 km ash column.
Killed ~1,369 people.
Pyroclastic flows killed 64 people.
Evacuation of 20,000 people prior to a major eruption.
The deadliest eruption in decades: 353 deaths, 350,000 evacuated.
Ongoing activity with ash emissions, lava flows, and pyroclastic avalanches.
Continued dome growth and pyroclastic flows on the southern flank. Several explosions recorded during the year.
Ongoing dome growth and pyroclastic density currents on the southern flank. Elevated seismicity and deformation recorded.
The largest eruption ever recorded. Killed ~71,000 people. Caused the 'Year Without a Summer' of 1816 worldwide.
Minor eruption.
Renewed fumarolic and seismic activity.
First eruption in 400 years.
Pyroclastic flows killed 16 people.
5 km ash column.
Eruption triggered lahars that destroyed bridges and roads.
Continuous eruptions with pyroclastic flows.
Ongoing activity with frequent eruptions and ash emissions. The tallest volcano in Java (3,676 m).
Ongoing explosive activity with frequent Vulcanian explosions and lava flows toward the Besuk Kobokan river.
Continued explosive activity with Vulcanian eruptions and pyroclastic flows toward Besuk Kobokan. Alert level maintained.
Heian period eruption.
Jo'an eruption generated large lava flows.
Hōei eruption, the last known. Covered Edo (Tokyo) in ash for weeks.
Largest eruption of the 20th century in Japan. Joined the island to the Ōsumi Peninsula.
Southwest flank eruption.
Near-daily eruptive activity. One of the most active volcanoes in the world.
Ongoing activity with multiple explosive eruptions and frequent ash columns.
Frequent explosive eruptions throughout the year, with ash plumes reaching several kilometres above the crater.
First eruption recorded in modern times.
Phreatic eruption without warning: 63 hikers killed. The worst volcanic disaster in modern Japan.
Second largest eruption of the 20th century. Killed 847 people. Cooled the planet by 0.5°C for two years.
Residual activity following 1991.
Buried the town of Cagsawa; 1,200 deaths.
79 deaths.
Evacuation of 80,000 people.
Lava flows and pyroclastic surges forced massive evacuations.
Ongoing activity with lava and ash emissions. The most perfectly shaped volcano in the world.
Historical eruption recorded in Viking sagas.
Eruption that lasted until 1823.
Paralyzed European air traffic for weeks, affecting 10 million passengers.
Destroyed Viking settlements. Known as 'The Gateway to Hell' in the Middle Ages.
13-month eruption.
Explosive eruption with lava flows.
Last major eruption recorded.
Devastating jökulhlaup (glacial flood).
Major eruption with a 20 km column.
Eruption with a 10 km column.
First eruption in 800 years on the Reykjanes Peninsula. Spectacular lava fountains and rivers visited by thousands of tourists.
Second eruption in the series, with more voluminous flows.
New fissures and lava flows threatened the town of Grindavík.
Multiple fissure eruptions in the Sundhnúkagígar system. Lava flows reached the defenses of Grindavík.
New fissure eruption on the Reykjanes Peninsula. Lava flows advanced north of the Svartsengi geothermal area.
Destroyed Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Stabiae under layers of ash and pyroclasts. ~16,000 deaths. Described by Pliny the Younger.
Killed ~3,000 people.
Destroyed Torre Annunziata.
Last known eruption. Destroyed Allied combat aircraft during World War II.
The largest historical eruption, destroying part of Catania.
Lateral fracture threatened Nicolosi.
Spectacular nocturnal lateral eruption visible from Catania.
Ongoing activity with lava flows and ash columns.
Frequent eruptive episodes with lava fountains and ash columns. The most active volcano in Europe.
Multiple paroxysmal eruptive episodes from the Southeast Crater. Lava flows and ash plumes recorded throughout the year.
Paroxysmal eruption.
Paroxysmal explosion killed one hiker and injured several tourists.
Continuous eruptive activity. Known as 'the lighthouse of the Mediterranean' for its nocturnal eruptions visible from the sea.
Uninterrupted Strombolian activity, as it has been for centuries. Regular explosions every 15–20 minutes.
Ongoing Strombolian activity from the summit craters. Near-continuous eruptions with lava fountaining and tephra ejection.
Eruption of the Native American historical period.
Catastrophic lateral collapse. 57 deaths. Reduced the volcano's height by 400 m in minutes.
New lava dome growth inside the crater.
Last recorded eruption.
Beginning of the Pu'u'ō'ō eruption, one of the longest in history: 35 continuous years.
Eruption in the lower East Rift Zone. Destroyed ~700 homes and covered the Leilani Estates area.
Eruption in the lava lake of Halemaʻumaʻu crater.
Ongoing eruptive activity at the summit.
New eruptive episodes at the summit with active lava lakes in Halemaʻumaʻu crater.
Summit eruption within Halemaʻumaʻu crater. Active lava lake and fissure activity on the East Rift Zone.
Lava flows reached the ocean, threatening Hilo.
22-day eruption.
First eruption in 38 years. Lava flows came within 3 km of the Daniel K. Inouye Highway.
First Yellowstone supereruption. One of the largest in Earth's history.
Second supereruption.
Last supereruption: created the current 72 × 55 km caldera.
Last known lava activity (rhyolitic lava flows).
Eruption recorded in Nahuatl pre-Hispanic sources.
Resumption of activity after decades of calm. Beginning of the current eruptive cycle.
Explosions and 3 km ash column. Maximum alerts issued for Mexico City.
Ongoing activity with exhalations and minor explosions.
Sustained activity with frequent steam and ash exhalations. On permanent alert.
Lava flows and lahars.
Violent eruption at 3 am. Evacuation of 3,000 people. 1.5 km lava fountains.
Ongoing activity with an active lava lake at the summit and gas emissions.
Active lava lake and persistent Strombolian activity from the summit crater. Elevated thermal anomalies observed.
Lahars reached the Pacific Ocean, traveling 300 km.
Eruption after 73 years of calm. Ash fell over Quito.
Orange alert maintained; explosive activity and ash emissions over the Andean region.
Catastrophic lahar destroyed the city of Armero: 23,000 deaths. Tragedy ignored by authorities.
Minor eruption with ash emissions.
Sustained activity with ash emissions. Volcanic alert maintained for surrounding municipalities.
Major explosive eruption.
Pyroclastic flow killed 194 people. The worst volcanic disaster in Guatemala in decades. Destroyed entire villages.
Ongoing activity with lava flows and frequent ash columns.
Periodic paroxysmal eruptions. One of the most active volcanoes in Central America, in near-constant eruption.
Lava lake drained in less than 1 hour. 70+ deaths.
Lava flows destroyed part of Goma. 147 deaths, 400,000 displaced.
Nocturnal lateral eruption. Lava flows reached 2 km from Goma.
Lahar destroyed a railway bridge, causing a train crash: 151 deaths.
Major eruption that forced ski slopes to close.
Crater lake overflow.
Minor eruption.
Phreatic eruption without warning. 22 tourists killed. Tragedy of enormous international media impact.
One of the largest eruptions of the 21st century at this volcano.
Multiple eruptions throughout the year.
Frequent activity; one of the most active volcanoes in the world.
New fissure eruptions with lava rivers in the caldera. Erupts several times a year.
Eruption began 13 February 2026 and stopped 12 April 2026 after three active phases. Lava flows spread across the Enclos Fouqué caldera.
The Minoan eruption, one of the largest of the Holocene. Possible origin of the Atlantis myth. Destroyed Minoan civilization.
Submarine eruption formed a new island.
Last known eruption.
Major eruption with lava flows.
Last recorded eruption, from the Chinyero flank.
Eruption at San Juan.
Eruption at Teneguía.
85-day eruption. Destroyed ~3,000 buildings, buried 1,000 ha under lava. €900M in losses.
Dome collapse: largest eruption of the 20th century in Kamchatka.
Powerful eruption with a 20 km column. Ash over Ust-Kamchatsk. Extensive pyroclastic flows.
Strong explosive activity with ash plumes reaching 10–15 km. Dome growth continued on the active lava dome.
First documented modern eruption, forming a new island.
The most powerful eruption of the 21st century. Transoceanic tsunami. The atmospheric shockwave circled the Earth twice.
Captain Cook documented it during his Pacific exploration.
Continuous Strombolian eruption. Has been erupting almost uninterruptedly for ~800 years.
Uninterrupted Strombolian activity with explosions visible from the coast. A unique tourist destination.
Near-continuous Strombolian eruptions from the summit crater, one of the longest-running active eruptions on Earth.
Sudden eruption after 400 years of inactivity. 87 deaths. Destroyed 3 villages.
Pyroclastic flows and lava. Almost continuous activity for two decades.
Last major eruption recorded.
Largest eruption of the 21st century here. Produces carbonatite lava unique in the active world: black when emerging, white when cooled.
Ongoing carbonatite lava activity. The only volcano with this type of active lava in the world.
Destroyed the city of Rabaul almost completely.
Explosive eruption captured by tourists aboard a cruise ship.
Eruption affected 90% of the island with SO2 gas. 250,000 people left without drinking water.
Eruption from the caldera.
Lava flows from the southern flank.
Eruptive activity on the southeast flank.
Destroyed the village of Chã das Caldeiras.
Lava flows destroyed two villages and covered their vineyards.
Major explosive eruption with lava flows.
Lava flows and frequent explosions.
Continued activity with ash emissions and minor lava flows.
Small eruption reported by explorers.
Last confirmed eruption.
Major eruption.
Two explosive eruptions in 24 hours without prior warning. 15 km column. Evacuation of 4,000 people.
Explosions and ash fall over Andean communities.
8 km eruptive column.
Intense explosive activity with ash columns. The most active volcano in Peru.
Major eruption after 80 years of calm. Evacuation of Baños.
Powerful eruption with a 15 km column.
Last major eruption recorded.
Last significant fumarolic activity ~8,000 years ago. The highest volcano in Asia.
Explosive eruption with an 11 km column.
Activity with ash column that affected air traffic.
Eruption killed 1,335 people.
Phreatomagmatic eruption with 200 deaths.
Violent eruption with a 15 km ash column and volcanic lightning. 500,000 evacuated.
Phreatic eruption with a 3 km column.

Last known volcanic activity in the Kibo crater. The tallest stratovolcano in Africa and the tallest freestanding mountain in the world (5,895 m). Its summit glaciers are disappearing due to climate change.
Major eruption that deposited ash across much of the Caucasus.
Last recorded eruption. The highest volcano in Europe (5,642 m) by the geographic definition that includes the Caucasus in Europe.
Eruption that formed the Kalahaku lava cone.
Last known eruption, near La Pérouse Bay. Its Hawaiian name means 'House of the Sun'. The crater is 11 km long and 800 m deep.
Last known eruption. Despite not being the highest peak above sea level, its summit is the farthest point on Earth's surface from the center of the Earth, due to the planet's equatorial bulge.
Eruption and associated earthquake destroyed the village of Arghuri. Armenian national symbol and, according to biblical tradition, where Noah's Ark came to rest.
Major eruption that generated a lahar traveling more than 50 km into the Sacramento Valley.
Last recorded eruption, observed by French explorers. Classified by the USGS as one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the US due to nearby population density.
Old Maid eruptive period that generated pyroclastic flows and lahars.
Last known eruptive activity. Visible from Portland (80 km). The USGS classifies it as a high-risk volcano.
Major eruption documented in Spanish colonial sources.
Last recorded eruption. The third highest peak in North America (5,636 m). Its Nahuatl name, Citlaltépetl, means 'Star Mountain'.
Beginning of the eruptive cycle after thousands of years of inactivity. First continental US volcano eruption of the 20th century.
Main eruption with a 9 km ash column and lahars. Was the most active US volcano until Mount St. Helens in 1980.
End of the eruptive cycle with residual fumarolic activity.

Last known eruptive activity ~6,500 years ago. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it is the tallest mountain in the world (10,210 m). Its summit hosts some of the most important astronomical observatories on the planet.
Last known volcanic activity. Its Nahuatl name means 'Sleeping White Woman' for its silhouette resembling a reclining woman seen from the Valley of Mexico. Has permanent retreating glaciers.
The volcano literally emerged from a cornfield on February 20th. Farmer Dionisio Pulido witnessed its birth. Within days it grew tens of meters tall.
Last eruption. Over 9 years of activity it buried the villages of Paricutín and San Juan Parangaricutiro. One of the few volcanoes in history whose birth was observed and documented by humans.
Last recorded volcanic activity. The highest volcano in the world (6,893 m). The border between Chile and Argentina passes exactly through its summit.
Major eruption that formed the caldera 2–3 million years ago. The largest intact volcanic caldera in the world (20 km diameter, 600 m deep). UNESCO World Heritage Site and home to ~25,000 animals.
Intense fumarolic activity observed by explorers.
Last recorded eruptive activity. In 1975 it experienced a notable increase in thermal emissions that led to evacuation studies. The second snowiest volcano in the US after Rainier.
The 'Millennium Eruption', one of the largest of the Holocene. Deposited ash as far as Japan and Russia. Formed Heaven Lake (Tianchi) in the summit caldera.
Eruption recorded in Korean and Chinese chronicles.
Eruption recorded in historical sources.
Last recorded eruption. The sacred mountain of the Korean and Manchurian peoples. Closely monitored for its reactivation potential.
Last recorded eruption, documented in the Goryeo Annals. The highest peak in South Korea (1,947 m). Jeju Island, formed by volcanic activity, is a UNESCO Natural Heritage Site.
Lava lake overflow with flows that destroyed nearby villages.
Ongoing lava lake activity.
Ongoing activity. One of the few volcanoes in the world with a permanent lava lake, active almost continuously since the 1960s.
Persistent lava lake activity in the summit caldera. Continued effusive eruptions on the caldera floor.
Beginning of the longest eruption of the 20th century in the Caribbean. Plymouth, the capital, was buried under ash and pyroclasts.
Pyroclastic flows killed 19 people. Permanent evacuation of the southern half of the island.
Last recorded eruptive activity. Plymouth remains the only abandoned capital in the modern world.
Eruption killed 1,680 people, the same day as Mount Pelée in Martinique.
Evacuation of 20,000 people.
Powerful explosive eruption with an 8 km column. 20,000 evacuated. Ash covered 95% of the island. Coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic.
Largest eruption of the 20th century. 25 km ash column.
Spectacular eruption with incandescent lava fountain at the summit, widely photographed.
Ongoing activity. The most active volcano in Mexico; has erupted more than 40 times since 1576.
Moderate explosive eruptions with ash columns and incandescent material ejected from the summit crater.
Phreatic eruption without warning killed 3 tourists at the crater rim.
Explosive eruption with an 11 km column.
Ongoing activity with SO2 emissions. Has the largest inhabited caldera in the world (25 × 18 km), with 50,000 people living inside.
Strombolian eruptions from the Nakadake crater. Ash fall reported in surrounding towns.

Last estimated eruption. The entire island is a volcanic edifice rising from the floor of the East Sea. Its mountainous interior and cliffs are the result of centuries of volcanic activity and marine erosion.
Catastrophic eruption that killed over 1,000 people and destroyed villages on Bali. One of the deadliest eruptions of the 20th century in Indonesia.
Eruption preceded by months of seismic unrest. Tens of thousands evacuated from Bali. Ash columns reached 3 km above the crater.
Continued intermittent explosive activity with ash plumes. Bali airport temporarily closed on multiple occasions.
Volcanic mudflows (lahars) triggered by crater lake expulsion killed over 5,000 people. One of the deadliest lahars in Indonesian history.
Explosive eruption with pyroclastic flows. Crater lake volume reduced significantly following the event.
Sudden explosive eruption ejected the crater lake in minutes. Ash fall reached Yogyakarta and Solo, 200 km away. Nearly 100,000 people evacuated.
Extended eruptive episode with ash columns up to 800 m. Surrounding villages evacuated and Tengger Caldera access restricted.
Increased Strombolian activity from the summit crater. Ash advisories issued for regional aviation.
Phreatic explosions and ash fall affected nearby communities in the Tengger Caldera area.
Major eruption from the Barujari cone inside the caldera. Lava flows and ash ejection into Segara Anak crater lake.
Eruption from the Barujari cone with lava flows reaching the crater lake. Lombok airport temporarily closed.
Eruption triggered by a magnitude 6.2 earthquake. Ash column reached 5 km. Several thousand tourists evacuated from the caldera.
Explosive eruption with ash columns reaching 3 km. Surrounding agricultural areas affected by ash fall.
Sudden eruption killed 24 hikers on the summit trails. One of the deadliest volcanic events in Indonesia in recent years.
Continued explosive activity following the 2023 eruption sequence. Alert level maintained at the highest status.
